front: What are the best-case, worst-case and average-case costs of a linear search for one name in a list?
back: Best $O(1)$, worst $O(n)$, average $O(n)$ (half the list on average).

front: What does $\lg n$ denote in the lecture's Big O notation?
back: The binary logarithm (base 2); $\log$ alone denotes base 10.

front: In a B tree search, how do we know a value does not exist?
back: The search reaches the leaf level without finding it.

front: In a B+ tree, what is the rule for values relative to a separator?
back: Values on the left are smaller; values on the right are larger than or equal to the separator.

front: Must a separator value in a B+ tree non-leaf node exist in the database?
back: No. A separator only guides the search, so a value like 20 can be a separator even if no record has 20.

front: In a B+ tree range query, when does the scan of sibling leaves stop?
back: When the next sibling's smallest value already exceeds the upper bound of the range.

front: What is the update cost of a B / B+ tree index?
back: $O(\lg n)$, the same order as its search cost.

front: What does it mean that a B / B+ tree is balanced?
back: The path length from the root to every leaf node is the same.

front: Can one table have more than one index?
back: Yes. A table can have multiple indices, e.g., one on module code and one on grade.

front: Why is the space overhead of an index smaller than the records themselves?
back: The index stores only pointers to records; there is always only one copy of the record contents.

front: How does an RDBMS query optimizer choose a query plan?
back: It keeps statistics about the database (e.g., number of records) and automatically picks the estimated best plan.

front: What are the two main challenges in handling database transactions?
back: Concurrency control (many users on the same data) and recovery (restoring contents after failure).

front: Why does an ATM wait for an "OK" acknowledgement from the central database after an update?
back: The network may drop a message; if no OK arrives in time, the ATM resends the message.

front: What defines a correct concurrent execution of transactions?
back: One equivalent to a serial execution, where transactions run one by one; any serial order is deemed correct.

front: Name two concurrency control methods other than two-phase locking.
back: Timestamp ordering and Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC).

front: Does a transaction holding a writelock on $x$ also need a readlock on $x$?
back: No. A writelock is an upgraded readlock, so it also permits reading.

front: What is the core principle of log-based recovery?
back: Save to the log before writing to the database system.

front: What three kinds of entries must a recovery log contain?
back: A record of each transaction's start, a record of its commit, and the update contents.

front: How does a blocking checkpoint work?
back: All database updates are stopped, a snapshot is taken, and recovery only scans back to the closest checkpoint.

front: Besides a snapshot, what does a fuzzy checkpoint record?
back: The list of transactions that are running at the time of the checkpoint.

front: What is the worst-case recovery cost with fuzzy checkpoints?
back: $O(n)$: scanning backwards to the first log entry, which only happens with a very short log or an unreasonably long transaction.

front: What is the primary function of the DISTINCT keyword in a SQL query?
back: It eliminates duplicate records from the query result set.

front: To remove duplicate major names from the Student table, complete the query: SELECT _____ Major FROM Student;
back: DISTINCT

front: In standard SQL, which comparison operator is used to test if a value is not equal to another value?
back: The $<>$ operator (or $\ne$).

front: How must string literal parameters be formatted in a SQL WHERE clause compared to integer parameters?
back: String parameters must be enclosed in quotes (e.g., 'Mary'), whereas integer parameters do not use quotes.

front: How does the AND logical operator differ from the OR logical operator in a SQL WHERE clause?
back: AND requires all combined conditions to be satisfied, whereas OR requires at least one condition to be satisfied.

front: Which logical operator is used to reverse or negate a condition in a SQL WHERE clause?
back: The NOT operator.

front: In a SQL ORDER BY clause, what is the default sorting direction if no direction keyword is specified?
back: Ascending order (ASC).

front: What keyword must be added after an attribute in an ORDER BY clause to sort results in descending order?
back: DESC

front: How does SQL evaluate an ORDER BY clause containing multiple columns, such as ORDER BY Grade DESC, Name DESC?
back: It sorts the results by Grade first, and uses Name in descending order as a tiebreaker for identical Grade values.

front: Where must the ORDER BY clause be placed in relation to the WHERE clause in a SQL statement?
back: The ORDER BY clause must be placed after the WHERE clause.

front: What is the function of the LIMIT clause in a SQL query?
back: It restricts the maximum number of records returned by the query.

front: What is the function of the OFFSET clause in a SQL query?
back: It skips a specified number of rows in the result set before returning any records.

front: What rows are returned by a query ending with LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10?
back: It skips the first 10 records and returns the 11th through 20th records.

front: Concept: CASE Statement
back: Definition: A conditional expression in SQL that evaluates conditions in order and returns a specific value when the first true condition is met.

front: In a SQL CASE statement, which keyword marks the end of the conditional expression block?
back: The END keyword.

front: In a CASE expression, which clause provides a default return value when none of the WHEN conditions are met?
back: The ELSE clause.

front: Complete the SQL CASE statement structure: CASE WHEN condition1 THEN result1 _____ default_result END
back: ELSE

front: How can you assign a column alias to the output of a CASE statement?
back: By placing the AS keyword followed by the alias name immediately after the END keyword.

front: What is the fundamental difference between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause regarding filtering order?
back: WHERE filters rows before the GROUP BY operation, while HAVING filters aggregated data after the GROUP BY operation.

front: In SQL logical execution order, which clause runs immediately before WHERE?
back: The FROM clause (including JOINs).

front: In SQL logical execution order, does ORDER BY execute before or after SELECT projection?
back: ORDER BY executes after the SELECT projection step.

front: Complete the filtering condition to find records where ID is greater than 100 and less than 102: SELECT * FROM Student WHERE ID _____ 100 _____ ID _____ 102;
back: > AND < (forming ID > 100 AND ID < 102)

front: Which SQL sub-language does `INSERT INTO` belong to?
back: DML (Data Manipulation Language), which adds and removes data.

front: Which SQL sub-language covers granting access to users?
back: DCL (Data Control Language).

front: Are SQL command keywords case-sensitive?
back: No. Commands are case-insensitive, although usernames and passwords are case-sensitive.

front: What does `DECIMAL(a, b)` declare?
back: A decimal number with $a$ total digits, $b$ of them after the decimal point, e.g., `DECIMAL(5, 2)` holds 347.88.

front: What is the difference between `CHAR(n)` and `VARCHAR(n)`?
back: `CHAR(n)` is fixed-length text of exactly $n$ characters; `VARCHAR(n)` is variable-length text of at most $n$ characters.

front: Which SQL data type holds large binary data such as images?
back: `BLOB`.

front: How does `NULL` differ from an empty string `''`?
back: `NULL` means the value does not exist or is unknown; `''` means there is a value and we know it is empty.

front: What SQL command creates an index on the Name and Year columns of Student?
back: `CREATE INDEX idx ON Student (Name, Year);`

front: How do you refer to an attribute when two joined tables share the same column name?
back: Use `[table name].[attribute name]`, e.g., `Student.StudentID`.

front: Is the `AS` keyword required when aliasing a table?
back: No. `FROM Student s` works the same as `FROM Student AS s`.

front: How does SQL process a query that joins three tables?
back: Each join is done sequentially: Student joins Result, then that result joins Module.

front: What requirements must two queries meet to be combined with `UNION`, `INTERSECT` or `EXCEPT`?
back: The same number of columns with compatible data types.

front: How does `UNION ALL` differ from `UNION`?
back: `UNION ALL` is a multiset union that keeps duplicates; `UNION` is a set operation that removes them.

front: What does a `WITH` statement do?
back: It names a sub-query as a temporary table before the main query, e.g., `WITH T AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM T`.

front: What is the syntax for modifying existing rows in SQL?
back: `UPDATE table_name SET column1 = value1, ... WHERE condition;`

front: Where do `DISTINCT` and `LIMIT / OFFSET` fall in SQL's logical execution order?
back: After `SELECT` projection: `DISTINCT`, then `ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT / OFFSET` last.

front: Name two advantages and two limitations of SQLite (besides database-level locking).
back: Lightweight and embeddable; but single-node (not scalable, not for remote access) and no built-in authentication.

front: For `SELECT * FROM Student a, Result b WHERE a.ID = b.ID AND a.Name = 'Tom'`, what is the efficient execution strategy?
back: Filter `Name = 'Tom'` in Student first, then compute the join on far fewer records.

front: What does a BI dashboard provide?
back: An at-a-glance view of key performance indicators (KPIs).

front: Name the three key features of Power BI listed in the lecture.
back: Dashboards, reporting, and online analytical processing (OLAP).

front: Which tool do both Excel and Power BI use to extract, transform and load (ETL) data?
back: The Power Query Editor.

front: What engine do Excel's Power Pivot and Power BI's core share?
back: VertiPaq, an in-memory, column-based analytical engine.

front: What expression language do Excel and Power BI both use for calculated columns and measures?
back: DAX (Data Analysis Expressions).

front: How does the purpose of Excel differ from that of Power BI?
back: Excel is for spreadsheets and calculation; Power BI is for business intelligence: interactive reports and dashboards.

front: How do Excel and Power BI differ in data capacity?
back: Excel is limited (performance degrades around 1 million rows); Power BI is built for big data.

front: How does the data model differ between Excel and Power BI?
back: In Excel a data model (Power Pivot) is optional; in Power BI tables and their relationships are mandatory.

front: How do Excel and Power BI differ in data refresh and sharing?
back: Excel refreshes manually and shares files; Power BI refreshes automatically on schedules and shares via the cloud.

front: What is Business Intelligence (BI)?
back: A technology-driven process for analysing data and presenting actionable information.

front: List the five steps of the Power BI workflow in order.
back: Connect, Transform, Model, Calculate, Visualize & Publish.

front: Which Power BI component handles the Connect step?
back: Power Query: accessing data from sources such as databases, files and web APIs.

front: Which component and language handle the Transform step in Power BI?
back: The Power Query Editor, using the M language: cleaning, shaping, merging and preparing data (the ETL stage).

front: What is done in the Data Model View (the Model step)?
back: Defining relationships, setting data types, and creating hierarchies.

front: What is DAX used for in the Power BI workflow (the Calculate step)?
back: Creating measures (KPIs) and calculated columns for analysis.

front: Which components handle the Visualize & Publish step?
back: Report View and the Power BI Service: building interactive reports and sharing them with end-users.

front: Why is a transactional (OLTP) schema a poor basis for BI analysis?
back: It is optimized for data entry, not analysis, with many tables and complex joins.

front: What is the function of OLTP (Online Transactional Processing)?
back: To process database transactions and record them.

front: What are the requirements of an OLTP system?
back: Real-time, low-latency response; ACID compliance; and high throughput of concurrent transactions.

front: What is the purpose of OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)?
back: Interactive data analytics: exploring data to discover interesting findings, with fast responses to each action.

front: In a star schema, what is the central table called and what does it record?
back: The fact table; it records what happened (e.g. Enrollment).

front: What do dimension tables in a star schema provide?
back: Additional context to the facts: who, what, when, where (e.g. Student, Course, Location).

front: How does a snowflake schema differ structurally from a star schema?
back: Its dimension tables are normalized into child dimension tables.

front: What is normalization and what are its two aims?
back: The systematic organization of columns and tables to minimize data redundancy and improve data integrity.

front: Which schema is preferred for OLAP, and why?
back: The star schema: fewer joins give faster query performance.

front: What is the disk-space trade-off between star and snowflake schemas?
back: Star uses more space (redundancy in dimensions); snowflake is more space-efficient.

front: Contrast OLTP and OLAP workloads in terms of users and queries.
back: OLTP: many concurrent users running simple queries that modify a few records; OLAP: few users running complex, usually read-only aggregate queries.

front: Is strong (ACID) consistency necessary for OLAP?
back: No; OLAP reads from a data warehouse or lake, whereas ACID is very important for OLTP.

front: What is roll-up (drill-up) in OLAP?
back: Aggregating data to a higher level, e.g. grades A and B combined into Pass; the reverse of drill-down.

front: What is drill-down in OLAP?
back: Breaking data into more detail, e.g. adding a dimension such as sex to a grade count.

front: What is drill-through in OLAP?
back: Navigating from a summary view to a detailed report page filtered to a specific context.

front: What is slicing in OLAP?
back: Adding filters to focus on particular value(s) of some attribute(s), e.g. only grade A records.

front: What is the difference between drill-down and slicing?
back: Drill-down keeps the same data source at finer detail; slicing filters out part of the data.

front: Name the techniques that make VertiPaq fast.
back: In-memory columnar storage, compression, multi-threading, and caching.

front: What is the idea behind an OLAP data cube?
back: Pre-compute common intermediate results (aggregates over a known feature set $F$) so OLAP actions are answered from the cube.

front: What assumptions must hold for building a data cube?
back: The feature set $F$ is known and small, and its value combinations are far fewer than the database records.

front: What are the limitations of data cubes?
back: A new feature requires recomputing the cube, and new data needs maintenance to update it.

front: In SQL terms, what is generating a data cube equivalent to?
back: A group-by query over the chosen features, with a count per group.

front: Compare VertiPaq and a data cube on flexibility and speed.
back: VertiPaq handles any query with good general speed; a cube is near-instant but only for anticipated queries.

front: How can a data cube be integrated with Power BI simply?
back: Load the cube's cell data instead of the raw data, so Power BI manages far fewer records.

front: Where do you import data in Power BI, and what sources were shown?
back: Home > Get data; databases (e.g. Microsoft SQL) and files (CSV, Excel).

front: When an imported CSV's column headers are not recognized, how do you fix it?
back: In the Power Query Editor, use the first row as column names.

front: Which Power Query feature joins tables, and where is it?
back: Merge Queries, under Home > Combine > Merge Queries.

front: What does a Left Anti Join return?
back: Records in A that have no match in B.

front: What does a Left Outer Join return?
back: All records of A, with matching B values or nulls where there is no match.

front: Why is it natural for data to be distributed in the first place?
back: Data naturally resides where it is generated, so storing it at multiple sites follows its origin.

front: How does a distributed database improve reliability and availability?
back: Data is replicated across multiple nodes, so the failure of one site does not halt the entire system.

front: Name two ways a distributed database improves performance.
back: Queries can run in parallel across multiple sites, and processing closer to the data reduces network latency.

front: What is the economic argument for a distributed database?
back: It is often more cost-effective to connect many smaller, cheaper machines than to buy a single monolithic mainframe.

front: What is the overall goal of a distributed database system?
back: To host the database on multiple machines (nodes) while appearing to users as if it were a single, centralized database.

front: What is location transparency, and how can it be achieved for a service?
back: Users need not know where data is stored; one idea is mapping a domain name to different IP addresses depending on the requester's location.

front: What are the three main challenges of distributed database systems listed in the lecture?
back: Security across sites and networks, distributed query processing (minimising network traffic while optimising response time), and distributed transaction management (ensuring ACID across network boundaries).

front: What is fragmentation (sharding)?
back: Partitioning a table into smaller, non-overlapping subsets that can be stored at different sites.

front: What three decisions does fragmentation and replication design involve?
back: What data to store, where to store it, and how many copies to keep.

front: What is horizontal fragmentation (HF)?
back: Splitting a relation by rows (records); MongoDB and Google Spanner are examples of systems that use it.

front: What is vertical fragmentation (VF)?
back: Splitting a relation by columns (attributes); in an RDBMS it can be implemented at application level, and MonetDB is an example.

front: What is mixed fragmentation?
back: Applying both horizontal and vertical fragmentation; it is the most complex but most flexible option.

front: Which fragmentation suits `SELECT * FROM T WHERE EmployeeID = 107`, and why?
back: Horizontal fragmentation, because the whole record sits at one site and only that site needs to be queried.

front: Which fragmentation suits `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM T WHERE Salary > 50000`, and why?
back: Vertical fragmentation, because the query needs only the `Salary` column and can read just the fragment holding it.

front: How is the original table reconstructed under HF versus VF?
back: HF fragments are recombined with a UNION; VF fragments are recombined with a JOIN (on the key), which is more complex.

front: What is the data-locality advantage of horizontal fragmentation?
back: An entire record is stored at its most frequently accessed site, e.g. Hong Kong account records kept in the HK database.

front: What are the two advantages of vertical fragmentation?
back: Queries read only the columns they need, and sensitive columns (e.g. salary) can be isolated on a high-security server.

front: What are the benefits of replication?
back: Availability (another copy survives a failure), reduced latency (read the closest copy) and parallelism (reads run in parallel).

front: What are the costs of replication?
back: Update overhead, since every update must be propagated to all copies, and complex concurrency control to keep the copies mutually consistent.

front: What is the dominant cost factor in distributed query processing?
back: Network communication (latency and volume), so the goal is to minimise data transfer.

front: List the four steps of distributed query processing.
back: Query decomposition, distributed optimisation and localisation, local execution, and result reconstruction.

front: What happens in the localisation step of distributed query processing?
back: The system determines which site (fragment) holds the required data and transforms the query where appropriate.

front: With HF on `EmployeeID <= 105` (Site 1) and `> 105` (Site 2), how is `WHERE EmployeeID = 107` processed?
back: Only Site 2 is relevant, so the query is sent there alone; no reconstruction is needed because there is one local result.

front: With the same HF split, how is `WHERE Department = 'Sales' AND IsFullTime = True` processed?
back: The query is sent to both sites, and the local results are combined with a UNION.

front: What is a distributed transaction, and what is its goal?
back: A transaction involving data at more than one site (e.g. a transfer between accounts at different sites); all sites must agree to commit or abort despite partitions or failures.

front: What is centralized two-phase locking?
back: One site is designated as the central lock manager for all data items.

front: What is primary copy two-phase locking?
back: Each data item has its own central manager (its primary copy), and different items may have different managers.

front: How does distributed two-phase locking grant a lock?
back: By majority vote: the transaction proceeds when more than half of the nodes holding the item grant the lock.

front: What are the drawbacks of centralized 2PL?
back: Congestion at the central node, scale limited by that node, higher network cost than using the closest node, and a single point of failure.

front: What are the advantages of centralized 2PL over the other 2PL variants?
back: Deadlocks are easy to detect, and it is the easiest to implement.

front: In primary copy 2PL, what role do the non-primary copies play?
back: Reads go to the primary copy only; the other copies serve as backups.

front: What are the drawbacks of primary copy 2PL?
back: Congestion on hot data items, no account of geographical location, and a single point of failure per data item.

front: What are the trade-offs of distributed 2PL?
back: It improves availability (no single point of failure, no distant manager) but sends far more messages, is complex to implement, and makes deadlock detection hard.

front: Why is deadlock detection hard outside centralized 2PL?
back: A wait cycle can span sites (T1 waits for T2 at site 1, T2 waits for T1 at site 2), and no single site sees the loop without communicating.

front: How can unique transaction timestamps be generated in a distributed system?
back: Centrally, by one site assigning them, or in a distributed way by concatenating a local timestamp with a unique site identifier: $TS(T) = \text{Local\_Timestamp} \,\|\, \text{Site\_ID}$.

front: In timestamp-based protocols, which transaction is "older" and which has priority?
back: The transaction with the smaller timestamp is older, and older transactions have priority over younger ones.

front: Wound-Wait: what happens when T1 requests a lock held by T2?
back: If T1 is older, it wounds T2 (T2 is rolled back); if T1 is younger, T1 waits.

front: Wait-Die: what happens when T1 requests a lock held by T2?
back: If T1 is older, T1 waits; if T1 is younger, T1 dies (is rolled back).

front: Why can neither Wound-Wait nor Wait-Die deadlock?
back: In Wound-Wait an older transaction never waits for a younger one; in Wait-Die a younger one never waits for an older one, so no wait cycle can form.

front: Compare the abort behaviour of Wound-Wait and Wait-Die.
back: Wound-Wait has a lower abort rate but costlier aborts (a wounded transaction may have done much work); Wait-Die aborts more often but cheaply, since young transactions die early.

front: What is the downside of Wound-Wait and Wait-Die compared with plain 2PL?
back: They may cause unnecessary aborts, whereas 2PL does not (though 2PL can deadlock).

front: In Timestamp Ordering, what are $RTS(X)$ and $WTS(X)$?
back: The timestamps of the youngest transaction that successfully read X and the youngest that successfully wrote X, respectively.

front: What is the core idea of Timestamp Ordering (T/O)?
back: If T1 has a smaller timestamp than T2, T1 must take effect before T2.

front: T/O read rule: what happens when a transaction with timestamp $t$ reads X?
back: If $t < WTS(X)$ it is too late and rolls back; otherwise the read succeeds and $RTS(X) := \max(RTS(X), t)$.

front: T/O write rule: what happens when a transaction with timestamp $t$ writes X?
back: If $t < RTS(X)$ it rolls back; else if $t < WTS(X)$ the write is ignored (Thomas Write Rule); otherwise $WTS(X) := t$.

front: What is the Thomas Write Rule?
back: An outdated write ($t < WTS(X)$ but $t \ge RTS(X)$) is simply ignored, because it does not affect correctness.

front: What are the pros and cons of basic T/O?
back: No locking and no waiting, but a high abort rate and possible cascading aborts.

front: How does Multiversion Timestamp Ordering (MVTO) handle reads?
back: It keeps all versions of the data, so a read never aborts: it just returns the right version for its timestamp.

front: How does MVTO handle writes?
back: It checks against the youngest read timestamp; if the write is too late it aborts, otherwise a new version is added.

front: What are the costs and remaining weakness of MVTO?
back: Higher storage for multiple versions and complex garbage collection of old versions; write aborts remain, typically late in a transaction.

front: How do MVCC and MVTO relate?
back: MVCC is the general approach; MVTO is one specific MVCC algorithm. There is no single standard MVCC algorithm.

front: How does PostgreSQL combine MVCC and locking?
back: MVCC handles read-write conflicts, while locking handles write-write conflicts, schema changes (whole table) and explicit `SELECT FOR UPDATE` row locks.

front: What is the purpose of the Raft algorithm?
back: It is a consensus, fault-tolerance protocol that handles failures in a distributed environment and increases availability.

front: Does Raft distribute the database workload?
back: No. A Raft group serves one partition/shard; the leader carries extra work (e.g. synchronisation), and the goal is fault tolerance.

front: What roles do nodes play in a Raft group?
back: The nodes elect one unique leader; the others are followers.

front: How does Raft handle a client write in normal operation?
back: The client talks only to the leader, which sends the update to the followers; the operation is done once a majority acknowledges it.

front: How does Raft detect and recover from leader failure?
back: The leader sends periodic heartbeats; if it is found dead, a new leader is elected, and a recovered node resynchronises data from the group.

front: Define the three CAP properties.
back: Consistency: every read gets the most recent write or an error. Availability: every request to a non-failing node gets a response. Partition tolerance: the system keeps working despite dropped or delayed messages between nodes.

front: How does the C in CAP differ from the C in ACID?
back: CAP consistency is about data freshness across sites; ACID consistency is about data correctness.

front: What does the CAP theorem state, and who proved it?
back: A distributed system can provide at most two of C, A and P; Brewer conjectured it in 2000, and Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002.

front: Which kind of system is CA?
back: A traditional centralized DBMS; once a system is distributed, partition tolerance forces a trade-off between C and A.

front: What does a CP system do when it cannot be sure of the latest data?
back: It returns an error (sacrificing availability) rather than a possibly stale answer.

front: What does an AP system do during a partition?
back: It always returns an answer but cannot promise it is the latest (sacrificing consistency).

front: How can MongoDB be configured as CP or AP?
back: Write-majority makes it CP (unavailable when a majority cannot communicate); minimal write (primary acknowledgement only) makes it AP, where a new primary may serve old data and ACID is not guaranteed.

front: What does BASE stand for?
back: Basically Available, Soft-state, Eventually consistent: a relaxed version of ACID for AP systems.

front: What does "eventually consistent" mean?
back: If the system runs long enough after some writes, the state becomes known and all further reads of an item return the same value.

front: When is BASE acceptable and when is ACID still needed?
back: BASE suits tasks tolerant of stale reads (e.g. summarising news); ACID remains essential for cases like bank account transactions.

front: What is a NewSQL system?
back: A modern distributed RDBMS aiming for high scalability with distributed ACID (essentially CP) using familiar SQL; NewSQL is not a language.

front: What does NoSQL stand for, and what class of system does it describe?
back: Not Only SQL: a broad class of non-relational DBMS, often with a flexible schema, although some still use a table structure.

front: Name the example system the lecture gives for each NoSQL type: graph, column-oriented, wide-column, in-memory, search engine, document.
back: Neo4j, KDB, Cassandra, Redis, Elasticsearch, and MongoDB (covered in the next chapter).

front: A graph fits in an edge table, so what is the problem with using an RDBMS for it?
back: Joins are expensive, and discovering relationships between nodes requires a large number of joins.

front: What is index-free adjacency?
back: Storing pointers between connected nodes directly, which gives graph databases constant traversal time.

front: How does breadth-first search explore a graph, and what is an example application?
back: It explores all direct neighbours at depth 1 before moving to depth 2, and so on; for example, checking whether a user is within a certain distance of another user on a social network.

front: What does PageRank measure, and what is an example application?
back: The relative importance or influence of nodes in a network; for example, identifying key opinion leaders on social media.

front: What are weakly connected components, as defined in the lecture?
back: Subgraphs where every pair of nodes is reachable from one another; their number equals the number of islands.

front: How is the graph built to detect someone operating hundreds of fake accounts?
back: Each account is a node, and an edge joins two accounts sharing a value on one or more features (IP, credit card, Wi-Fi, delivery address); the fake accounts form a big weakly connected component.

front: What three techniques reduce false positives in graph-based fraud detection?
back: Filtering supernodes such as public computers, adding weights and a connectivity threshold, and only considering activities within a tight time window.

front: How does community detection by label propagation work?
back: Each node starts with a unique label and iteratively adopts the majority label among its immediate neighbours until convergence.

front: What does the local clustering coefficient measure, and what is an example application?
back: How close a node's immediate neighbours are to forming a complete graph; it is used in spam and fake account detection.

front: What are the three components of an RDF record, and what is its query language?
back: Subject, predicate and object; it is queried with SPARQL, the query language of the Semantic Web.

front: What is the core difference between a standard RDBMS and a column-oriented database?
back: An RDBMS stores data on disk by rows; a column-oriented database stores it by columns.

front: With 3 values per disk I/O, why does summing one column of a 3-row, 4-column table take 3 I/Os in an RDBMS but 1 in a column store?
back: The RDBMS has the column's values spread across the row-ordered data, whereas the column store keeps them together in one block.

front: With 3 values per disk I/O, how many I/Os does inserting a 4-value record take in each storage layout?
back: An RDBMS may need 2, while a column-oriented database needs 4, one for each column.

front: Why can column-based storage achieve a higher compression rate?
back: Data within the same column are of very similar nature; this lowers storage cost and speeds up processing.

front: What does run-length encoding produce for `F, F, F, M, M, F, F`?
How does dictionary encoding compress a district column?
back: It stores each distinct value as a small code plus a lookup, so Sha Tin, Central, Sha Tin, Tai Po becomes 1, 2, 1, 3 with the dictionary Sha Tin→1, Central→2, Tai Po→3.

front: How do an RDBMS and a column-oriented database compare on reads and writes?
back: An RDBMS is write-optimized; a column-oriented database is read-optimized, so more efficient for reads and less efficient for writes.

front: What is the purpose of a wide-column database, and which system did the idea originate from?
back: To be highly scalable through horizontal scaling; it originates from Google Bigtable (OSDI 2006), with Cassandra and HBase as examples.

front: What is the Bigtable data model?
back: A map `(row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string`: given the row ID, column ID and timestamp, you get the data contents, so different versions can be retrieved.

front: What is notable about the query language of Cassandra?
back: CQL is SQL-like, but it has no JOIN operator.

front: How does a Log-Structured Merge-tree handle writes?
back: It buffers incoming writes in memory, occasionally flushes them to disk as immutable sorted records, and continuously merges and compacts them in the background, cleaning up deleted or outdated records.

front: What are the advantages of a wide-column database?
back: Massive horizontal scalability with the same underlying schema for all, fast write throughput from append-only mode (no locking), and no null overhead.

front: What are the problems of a wide-column database?
back: Poor support for queries needing joins, higher read latency than an RDBMS because of the effort to find the latest data in LSM trees, and only eventual consistency.

front: Give the benchmark read/write speeds that motivate an in-memory database.
back: Magnetic hard disk 80–160 MB/s, SSD 200–550 MB/s, RAM 2–20 GB/s.

front: What querying limitations does Redis have as a key-value store?
back: It indexes only the key, with no secondary index on other fields, so its querying power is limited.

front: What are the two Redis persistence mechanisms?
back: Snapshots of the dataset at specified intervals, and AOF, which logs every write so it can be replayed at startup; they can also be combined, or persistence turned off.

front: Why is B-tree indexing unsuitable for an in-memory database, and what is preferred?
back: B-trees are designed to be I/O optimal and are suboptimal in memory; a hash table is preferred, with $O(1)$ access but no range queries.

front: What is NVRAM, and how could Redis use it?
back: RAM that keeps data when the power is off but is slower than volatile RAM; it could serve as a faster layer for backup and recovery, not as primary memory.

front: Give three use cases for an in-memory database.
back: User session management, leaderboards in gaming, and high-frequency trading.

front: What is the key component of Elasticsearch?
back: An inverted index, which maps words to document IDs.

front: What does each component of the Elastic Stack (ELK) do?
back: Logstash is a data pipeline ingesting from multiple sources, Elasticsearch is the core engine, and Kibana is a frontend interface.

front: List the stages of the text analysis pipeline in order.
back: Character filter, tokenizer, normalization, stopword filter, stemming filter; a synonym filter can also replace or add tokens.

front: What is the formula for TF-IDF, and how do the textbook and scikit-learn versions of TF differ?
back: $\text{TF-IDF}(t,d)=\text{TF}(t,d)\times\text{IDF}(t)$. Textbook TF is the count of $t$ in $d$ divided by the total terms in $d$; scikit-learn TF is just the count.

front: How do the textbook and scikit-learn versions of IDF differ?
back: Textbook: $\log_{10}\left(\frac{N}{\text{df}(t)}\right)$. Scikit-learn: $\ln\left(\frac{N+1}{\text{df}(t)+1}\right)+1$.

front: In the lecture's 3-document corpus, what is the scikit-learn IDF of "cat" (in all 3) and of "chased" (in 1)?
back: $\ln(4/4)+1=1$ for "cat" and $\ln(4/2)+1=\ln(2)+1$ for "chased".

front: What are the problems of TF-IDF?
back: TF is counted linearly with no saturation, normalization is insufficient so longer documents are favoured, and there are no hyperparameters to tune.

front: What two limitations of TF-IDF does BM25 address?
back: Term frequency saturation, through a TF function capping how fast frequency raises the score, and length normalization, through tuneable parameters.

front: What is fuzzy search in Elasticsearch?
back: Returning results for similar words as well, with similarity measured by edit distance; it handles typos such as "box" for "fox".

front: What does an embedding model do?
back: It is a neural network mapping data (text, image or other types) to a dense vector, so that semantically similar inputs have close vectors.

front: What are the steps of semantic search in a vector database?
back: Chunk the text and embed each chunk into a vector, embed the query, then run a k nearest neighbour search for the closest data vectors.

front: What are cosine similarity and cosine distance?
back: Cosine similarity is $\frac{x\cdot y}{|x||y|}=\cos\theta$, with $\theta$ the angle between the vectors; cosine distance is $1$ minus the cosine similarity.

front: When does cosine similarity reduce to a dot product?
back: When the embedding model outputs unit vectors, because their magnitude is 1.

front: How does the Inverted File Index (IVF) speed up kNN search?
back: The data is clustered by K-means and the search narrows to candidate clusters; average $O(\sqrt{n})$, worst case $O(n)$, with approximate results.

front: How are the layers of HNSW structured?
back: Each higher layer is a sparser subset of the lower one, the ground layer contains all vectors, and each node keeps edges to its neighbours in each layer.

front: How does an HNSW search proceed?
back: From the top layer it greedily hops to the closest neighbours, then moves to a denser layer; at the ground layer it refines the closest neighbours and returns the top K.

front: What is the advantage of IVF over HNSW, and of HNSW over IVF?
back: IVF uses less memory; HNSW searches faster, $O(\lg n)$ against $O(\sqrt{n})$, and needs no re-training, whereas IVF requires K-means clustering.

front: Concept: Classification
back: Definition: A predictive task that learns a model to map input attributes to a categorical class attribute. Example: Classifying credit card transactions as either legitimate or fraudulent.

front: What type of target attribute does classification aim to predict?
back: A discrete or categorical class attribute.

front: What is the primary goal of the classification task in data mining?
back: To construct a model that accurately predicts the class label of unlabeled data based on its input attributes.

front: How is a classification model learned using historical data?
back: By analyzing a training set composed of records with known attribute values and pre-assigned class labels.

front: What are two examples of classification applied in cybersecurity and medical diagnosis?
back: Identifying network intruders in cyberspace and predicting whether tumor cells are benign or malignant.

front: In a credit card fraud detection classification model, what constitutes the class attribute?
back: The binary label indicating whether a historical transaction was fraudulent or fair.

front: How does customer churn prediction utilize classification modeling?
back: It uses demographic and behavioral customer attributes to predict the categorical decision label of whether a customer will buy or not buy a product.

front: Concept: Regression
back: Definition: A predictive task that estimates the value of a continuous variable based on other variables using a linear or nonlinear dependency model. Example: Predicting sales amounts of a new product based on advertising expenditure.

front: How does regression differ from classification with respect to the target variable?
back: Regression predicts a continuous-valued variable, whereas classification predicts a categorical class attribute.

front: What is an environmental science example of a regression task?
back: Predicting wind velocities as a function of continuous atmospheric variables like temperature, humidity, and air pressure.

front: What is a financial application of regression modeling?
back: Time series prediction of stock market indices.

front: Concept: Clustering
back: Definition: A descriptive task that groups data objects such that objects within the same group are similar and objects in different groups are distinct. Example: Subdividing retail customers into market segments based on demographic and lifestyle data.

front: In cluster analysis, intra-cluster distances are _____ while inter-cluster distances are _____.
back: minimized; maximized

front: Is cluster analysis categorized as a predictive or descriptive data mining method?
back: Descriptive

front: How is document clustering applied in web news services like Google News?
back: By grouping articles that share frequent key terms and high content similarity into distinct news topics.

front: What scientific application uses K-means clustering to analyze earth observation data?
back: Partitioning Sea Surface Temperature (SST) and Net Primary Production (NPP) datasets into clusters reflecting the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

front: Concept: Association Rule Discovery
back: Definition: A descriptive task that extracts dependency rules to predict the occurrence of an item based on the occurrences of other items in a transaction dataset. Example: Discovering that retail customers who buy diapers and milk are also likely to buy beer.

front: In market-basket analysis, what does an association rule like $\{\text{Milk}\} \rightarrow \{\text{Coke}\}$ indicate?
back: That transactions containing milk have a strong statistical likelihood of also containing Coke.

front: How can retailer management use an association rule where Bagels are in the antecedent and Potato Chips are in the consequent?
back: They can design joint sales promotions or optimize shelf placement to boost the sales of Potato Chips.

front: How is association rule discovery applied in medical informatics?
back: It discovers frequent combinations of patient symptoms and diagnostic test results that are associated with specific diseases.

front: Data mining tasks are broadly categorized into _____ methods and _____ methods.
back: predictive; descriptive

front: What distinguishes predictive data mining tasks from descriptive data mining tasks?
back: Predictive methods use variables to forecast unknown values, whereas descriptive methods find human-interpretable patterns that summarize the data.

front: What is a widely used definition of data mining as an extraction process?
back: The non-trivial extraction of implicit, previously unknown and potentially useful information from data.

front: Besides predictive modeling, clustering and association rules, what fourth core data mining task is listed?
back: Anomaly detection.

front: Name three data characteristics that make traditional data analysis techniques unsuitable for data mining.
back: Data that is large-scale, high dimensional, heterogeneous, complex or distributed (any three).

front: From a scientific viewpoint, what two things does data mining help scientists with?
back: Automated analysis of massive datasets, and hypothesis formation.

front: From a commercial viewpoint, why do companies turn to data mining?
back: Lots of data is collected and warehoused, computers are cheaper and more powerful, and competitive pressure pushes firms to offer better, customized services (e.g. in CRM).

front: What two broad purposes do applications of cluster analysis serve?
back: Understanding (e.g. grouping related documents, genes or stocks) and summarization (reducing the size of large data sets).

front: In clustering-based market segmentation, how is the clustering quality measured?
back: By observing the buying patterns of customers in the same cluster versus those in different clusters.

front: In supermarket shelf management, what data is processed to find items bought together?
back: Point-of-sale data collected with barcode scanners.

front: What three general benefits do big data technology and analytics offer society?
back: Better understanding of problems, evidence-based solutions, and reduced costs.

front: What lesson does the 2010 Haiti earthquake response illustrate about big data in disaster management?
back: Data quality is paramount for prioritizing information and minimizing incorrect use of limited rescue resources.

front: What is an attribute, and what other names is it known by?
back: A property or characteristic of an object; also called a variable, field, characteristic, dimension or feature.

front: What other names are used for a data object?
back: Record, point, case, observation, sample, entity or instance.

front: What four properties/operations determine an attribute's type?
back: Distinctness, order, meaningful differences, and meaningful ratios.

front: Which properties does each attribute type possess: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio?
back: Nominal: distinctness; ordinal: + order; interval: + meaningful differences; ratio: all four, including meaningful ratios.

front: What distinguishes a discrete attribute from a continuous attribute?
back: A discrete attribute has a finite or countably infinite set of values (e.g. zip codes, counts); a continuous attribute takes real-number values (e.g. height).

front: How is document data represented as record data?
back: Each document becomes a term vector whose components are terms and whose values are the number of times each term occurs.

front: What is transaction data?
back: A special type of record data in which each transaction (e.g. one shopping trip) involves a set of items (the products bought).

front: Name the three types of missing-value mechanism.
back: Missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR).

front: What are the three ways of handling missing values?
back: Eliminate the data objects or variables, estimate the missing values, or ignore the missing value during analysis.

front: How does noise differ for objects versus attributes?
back: For objects, noise is an extraneous object; for attributes, noise is a modification of the original values.

front: When is data cleaning for duplicate data a major issue?
back: When merging data from heterogeneous sources, e.g. the same person appearing with multiple email addresses.

front: How are the ordinal dissimilarity and similarity between values $x$ and $y$ defined?
back: Map values to integers $0$ to $n-1$; $d = \frac{|x - y|}{n - 1}$ and $s = 1 - d$.

front: What is the Minkowski distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$?
back: $d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \left( \sum_{k=1}^{n} |x_k - y_k|^r \right)^{1/r}$, a generalization of Euclidean distance.

front: What is the Hamming distance?
back: The city-block ($L_1$) distance between two binary vectors: the number of bits that differ.

front: What is the supremum ($L_{\max}$ or $L_\infty$) distance?
back: The maximum absolute difference between any component of the two vectors: $\max_k |x_k - y_k|$.

front: What is the Mahalanobis distance?
back: $\text{mahal}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix, so it accounts for correlated attributes.

front: What three properties must a distance satisfy to be a metric?
back: Positive definiteness ($d \ge 0$, and $d = 0$ only if $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$), symmetry, and the triangle inequality $d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) \le d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) + d(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z})$.

front: What is the formula for cosine similarity of document vectors $d_1$ and $d_2$?
back: $\cos(d_1, d_2) = \frac{\langle d_1, d_2 \rangle}{\|d_1\| \, \|d_2\|}$

front: What is the entropy $H(X)$ of a variable with outcome probabilities $p_1, \dots, p_n$, and what is its range?
back: $H(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \log_2 p_i$, measured in bits, between $0$ and $\log_2 n$.

front: How is mutual information $I(X;Y)$ computed from entropies?
back: $I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y)$, where $H(X,Y)$ is the joint entropy.

front: What is the maximum mutual information for discrete variables $X$ and $Y$?
back: $\log_2(\min(n_X, n_Y))$, where $n_X$ and $n_Y$ are the numbers of values of $X$ and $Y$.

front: What does the Maximal Information Coefficient (MIC) do?
back: Applies mutual information to two continuous variables: try binnings with $n_X \times n_Y \le N^{0.6}$, normalize each MI by $\log_2(\min(n_X, n_Y))$, and take the highest value.

front: When combining similarities across mixed attribute types, when is the indicator $\delta_k$ set to $0$?
back: When attribute $k$ is asymmetric and both objects have value $0$, or when either object has a missing value for it.

front: What are the three purposes of aggregation?
back: Data reduction, change of scale (e.g. cities into regions, days into months), and more stable data with less variability.

front: When is a sample representative?
back: When it has approximately the same properties of interest as the original data set; then using it works almost as well as the full data.

front: What is the curse of dimensionality?
back: As dimensionality increases, data becomes increasingly sparse, so density and distance between points become less meaningful.

front: What is the goal of Principal Components Analysis (PCA)?
back: To find a projection that captures the largest amount of variation in the data.

front: What is binarization, and which analysis typically needs it?
back: Mapping a continuous or categorical attribute into one or more binary variables; association analysis, which needs asymmetric binary attributes.

front: What is the difference between unsupervised and supervised discretization?
back: Unsupervised discretization finds breaks in the data values alone (equal width, equal frequency, K-means); supervised discretization uses class labels to find breaks.

front: What is an attribute transformation?
back: A function that maps the entire set of values of an attribute to a new set of replacement values, so each old value can be identified with a new value.

front: What are summary statistics?
back: Numbers that summarize key properties of a dataset, such as frequency, location, and spread.

front: Why can summary statistics be computed efficiently on massive datasets?
back: Most summary statistics can be calculated in a single pass through the data.

front: How is the frequency of an attribute value defined in a dataset?
back: It is the percentage of times that specific attribute value occurs in the dataset.

front: What is the mode of an attribute?
back: The most frequently occurring attribute value in a dataset.

front: For which data type are the concepts of frequency and mode primarily used?
back: Categorical data.

front: For an attribute $x$, what does the $p\text{th}$ percentile ($x_p$) represent?
back: The value of $x$ such that $p\%$ of all observed values are less than $x_p$.

front: For continuous or ordinal data, what specific summary statistic corresponds to the 50th percentile?
back: The median.

front: What primary property of a dataset does the arithmetic mean quantify?
back: The location or central tendency of a set of data points.

front: How do extreme outliers affect the sample mean of a dataset?
back: They pull the mean toward them because the mean is very sensitive to extreme values.

front: Which measure of location provides a central estimate that is resistant to extreme outliers?
back: The median.

front: What is a trimmed mean?
back: A robust measure of location calculated by removing a specified percentage of the highest and lowest values before averaging.

front: How is the range of a numerical attribute calculated?
back: By taking the difference between the maximum value and the minimum value.

front: What property of a dataset is quantified by variance ($s_x^2$) and standard deviation ($s_x$)?
back: The spread or dispersion of a set of data points.

front: How do extreme outliers impact the variance and standard deviation of a dataset?
back: They significantly inflate both measures because variance and standard deviation are highly sensitive to extreme values.

front: Which measure of location—mean or median—is preferred when analyzing skewed data containing severe outliers?
back: The median, because it is robust against distortion from extreme values.

front: The measure of location most sensitive to extreme values in a dataset is the _____.
back: mean

front: The standard summary measure defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum values is the _____.
back: range

front: Why is the range vulnerable to misrepresenting the overall dispersion of a dataset?
back: Because it relies solely on the two extreme values, making it highly sensitive to outliers.

front: Which two statistics serve as the most common measures of spread for continuous numerical data?
back: Variance and standard deviation.

front: Why are percentiles generally preferred over frequency or mode for continuous attributes?
back: Continuous values rarely repeat exactly, making percentile thresholds far more useful for describing distribution.

front: What is data exploration?
back: A preliminary exploration of the data to better understand its characteristics.

front: How is visualization defined in the lecture?
back: The conversion of data into a visual or tabular format so that characteristics of the data and relationships among items or attributes can be analyzed or reported.

front: What two things can humans detect well when data is visualized?
back: General patterns and trends, and outliers and unusual patterns.

front: In the lecture's box plot, which percentiles mark the box and the whiskers?
back: The box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles with the 50th (median) inside; the whiskers end at the 10th and 90th percentiles.

front: What is a key use of placing several box plots side by side?
back: Comparing the distributions of different attributes.

front: In a histogram, what does the height of each bar indicate?
back: The number of objects whose values fall in that bin.

front: What can plots of similarity or distance matrices be used for?
back: Visualizing the relationships between objects.

front: How can a scatter plot display more than two attributes?
back: Use a 3D scatter plot, or encode additional attributes in the size, shape and colour of the markers.

front: In Bayesian classification, what formula calculates the posterior probability $P(Y \mid X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d)$ using Bayes' theorem?
back: $P(Y \mid X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d) = \frac{P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d \mid Y) P(Y)}{P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d)}$

front: Under the Bayes classification framework, what decision rule determines the predicted class label $Y$?
back: Select the class $Y$ that maximizes the product $P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d \mid Y) P(Y)$.

front: What fundamental assumption does the Naïve Bayes classifier make regarding feature attributes?
back: It assumes that all attributes $X_i$ are conditionally independent of each other given the class label $Y$.

front: How is the class-conditional probability $P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d \mid Y_j)$ simplified under the Naïve Bayes independence assumption?
back: $P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_d \mid Y_j) = \prod_{i=1}^{d} P(X_i \mid Y_j)$

front: How is the prior probability $P(y)$ of a class estimated from training data?
back: It is calculated as the fraction of overall training instances that belong to class $y$.

front: Using standard relative frequency, what is the formula for $P(X_i = c \mid y)$ for a categorical attribute?
back: $P(X_i = c \mid y) = \frac{n_c}{n}$, where $n_c$ is the count of class $y$ instances with $X_i = c$, and $n$ is the total count of class $y$ instances.

front: Why does a single conditional probability value of $P(X_i = c \mid y) = 0$ create a major issue in Naïve Bayes?
back: Multiplying by zero causes the overall class-conditional product and posterior probability for class $y$ to become zero.

front: Under what circumstance does a conditional probability estimate $P(X_i = c \mid y)$ evaluate to zero?
back: It occurs when an attribute value $c$ is completely absent from all training records belonging to class $y$.

front: How does Laplace smoothing modify the categorical conditional probability formula $P(X_i = c \mid y)$?
back: $P(X_i = c \mid y) = \frac{n_c + 1}{n + v}$, where $v$ is the total number of distinct values attribute $X_i$ can take.

front: In the Laplace estimation formula $P(X_i = c \mid y) = \frac{n_c + 1}{n + v}$, what does the variable $v$ represent?
back: It represents the total number of unique attribute values that feature $X_i$ can take.

front: What is the formula for the $m$-estimate approach to conditional probability smoothing in Naïve Bayes?
back: $P(X_i = c \mid y) = \frac{n_c + m p}{n + m}$

front: In the $m$-estimate formula $P(X_i = c \mid y) = \frac{n_c + m p}{n + m}$, what does the parameter $p$ represent?
back: It represents an initial prior estimate of the probability $P(X_i = c \mid y)$ known apriori.

front: In the $m$-estimate formula $P(X_i = c \mid y) = \frac{n_c + m p}{n + m}$, what does the parameter $m$ represent?
back: It is a hyper-parameter that determines the weight or confidence placed on the prior estimate $p$.

front: How can continuous attributes be adapted for Naïve Bayes using discretization?
back: The continuous value range is partitioned into discrete bins, transforming the attribute into an ordinal categorical feature.

front: When avoiding discretization, how does Naïve Bayes estimate $P(X_i \mid Y_j)$ for continuous attributes?
back: It assumes a continuous probability distribution, such as a normal Gaussian distribution, and estimates its parameters from training data.

front: What formula calculates $P(X_i \mid Y_j)$ when assuming a normal distribution for continuous attribute $X_i$?
back: $P(X_i \mid Y_j) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_{ij}^2}} e^{-\frac{(X_i - \mu_{ij})^2}{2\sigma_{ij}^2}}$

front: Which two parameters must be computed from training data to evaluate a continuous Gaussian probability density function for class $Y_j$?
back: The sample mean $\mu_{ij}$ and sample variance $\sigma_{ij}^2$ for attribute $X_i$ within class $Y_j$.

front: Why do redundant or highly correlated attributes negatively affect Naïve Bayes performance?
back: They violate the class conditional independence assumption and improperly bias the probability estimates.

front: How does the Naïve Bayes algorithm handle missing attribute values in data instances?
back: It ignores missing attribute entries when performing conditional probability calculations.

front: Why is Naïve Bayes robust against isolated noise points in a training dataset?
back: Because parameter estimations rely on probabilities averaged across the entire training dataset rather than localized boundaries.

front: Name four decision tree induction algorithms besides Hunt's algorithm.
back: CART, ID3, C4.5, SLIQ and SPRINT (any four).

front: What is the entropy of a node $t$ with class frequencies $p_i(t)$?
back: $\text{Entropy}(t) = -\sum_{i=0}^{c-1} p_i(t) \log_2 p_i(t)$

front: What is the misclassification error of a node $t$?
back: $\text{Error}(t) = 1 - \max_i p_i(t)$

front: How is the gain of a split defined, and which split is chosen?
back: $\text{Gain} = P - M$ (impurity before minus weighted impurity after); choose the test with the highest gain, i.e. the lowest $M$.

front: For a two-class problem, what are the maximum values of Gini, entropy and misclassification error?
back: Gini $0.5$, entropy $1$, error $0.5$, all at a 50/50 class split.

front: What is the difference between static and dynamic discretization of continuous attributes in decision trees?
back: Static discretizes once at the beginning; dynamic repeats the discretization at each node.

front: How does a binary decision split on a continuous attribute work, and what is its drawback?
back: It tests $(A < v)$ or $(A \ge v)$, considering all possible cuts to find the best; it can be computationally intensive.

front: What is the difference between pre-pruning and post-pruning?
back: Pre-pruning stops growing the tree early (early stopping rule); post-pruning grows the full tree and then trims nodes.

front: Why can greedy decision tree induction miss the best tree?
back: The space of possible trees is exponentially large, and greedy approaches make locally optimal splits.

front: What three things does a nearest-neighbor classifier require?
back: The set of labeled records, a distance metric, and the value of $k$.

front: Why can nearest-neighbor classifiers produce decision boundaries of arbitrary shape?
back: They are local classifiers: each prediction depends only on nearby training points.

front: How do irrelevant and redundant attributes affect $k$-NN?
back: Irrelevant attributes add noise to the proximity measure; redundant attributes bias it towards certain attributes.

front: Why is computing $k$-NN proximity on only the attributes present in both instances a poor fix for missing values?
back: It effectively uses a different proximity measure for each pair of instances, so the proximities are not comparable.

front: What does the arm-length and reading-skills example illustrate?
back: Conditional independence: the two are related overall, but independent once age is fixed.

front: What optimization problem does a linear SVM solve?
back: Minimize $\frac{\|\mathbf{w}\|^2}{2}$ subject to $y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + b) \ge 1$ for all training records.

front: How is a test record classified by a linear SVM once $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$ are found?
back: $f(\mathbf{z}) = \text{sign}(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{z} + b)$: $+1$ if $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{z} + b \ge 0$, else $-1$.

front: Why does SVM find a global optimum when many other methods do not?
back: Its learning problem is a convex optimization problem, whereas many other methods use greedy, locally optimal approaches.

front: What is generalization error in classification?
back: It is the expected error of a classification model over random records selected from the underlying data distribution.

front: How do training error and test error differ?
back: Training error is calculated on the training dataset, whereas test error is calculated on a separate, unseen test dataset.

front: What defines model underfitting in classification?
back: Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple, resulting in high errors on both the training set and the test set.

front: What defines model overfitting in classification?
back: Overfitting occurs when a model is overly complex, yielding a small training error but a high test error.

front: How does increasing the training sample size affect model overfitting?
back: Increasing training data size reduces the difference between training error and test error for a given model complexity.

front: What is the primary purpose of a validation set during model building?
back: A validation set is used to estimate generalization error and tune model complexity without exposing the test set.

front: How does Occam's Razor apply to classification model selection?
back: Given models with similar generalization error, Occam's Razor dictates choosing the simpler model over the more complex one.

front: What is the formula for classification accuracy using confusion matrix terms?
back: $\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{\text{TP} + \text{TN} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}}$

front: Why is standard accuracy a misleading performance metric for heavily imbalanced datasets?
back: A trivial model predicting only the majority class achieves high accuracy while failing to detect any rare class instances.

front: How does $k$-fold cross-validation partition and evaluate data?
back: It divides data into $k$ disjoint subsets, iteratively training on $k-1$ folds and testing on the remaining fold.

front: How does stratified cross-validation differ from standard $k$-fold cross-validation?
back: Stratified cross-validation guarantees that each fold maintains the same class label proportions as the original dataset.

front: What defines leave-one-out cross-validation?
back: It is an extreme form of $k$-fold cross-validation where $k$ equals the total sample size $n$, testing on one instance at a time.

front: Which performance metrics form the axes of an ROC curve?
back: The y-axis represents the True Positive Rate (TPR) and the x-axis represents the False Positive Rate (FPR).

front: What is the formula for True Positive Rate (TPR)?
back: $\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$

front: What is the formula for False Positive Rate (FPR)?
back: $\text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}$

front: In an ROC plot formatted as $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$, what does the coordinate $(0,0)$ represent?
back: It represents a classifier that predicts every record to belong to the negative class.

front: In an ROC plot formatted as $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$, what does the coordinate $(1,1)$ represent?
back: It represents a classifier that predicts every record to belong to the positive class.

front: In an ROC plot formatted as $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$, what does the coordinate $(1,0)$ represent?
back: It represents an ideal classifier with perfect true positive detection and zero false positives.

front: What performance level is indicated by the diagonal line in an ROC curve?
back: The diagonal line represents the expected performance of random guessing.

front: How is the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) interpreted for model quality?
back: An ideal classifier has an AUC of $1.0$, whereas random guessing yields an AUC of $0.5$.

front: How are continuous classifier outputs used to construct a discrete step ROC curve?
back: Test records are sorted by score in decreasing order, and unique scores serve as thresholds to compute $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$ points.

front: What defines a class imbalance problem in data mining?
back: It occurs when records from one majority class heavily outnumber instances of a rare target class.

front: What is the cost matrix notation $C(i|j)$?
back: $C(i|j)$ denotes the cost associated with misclassifying an instance of actual class $j$ as predicted class $i$.

front: In cost-sensitive classification, under what condition is a test record classified as positive?
back: A record is classified as positive when the expected cost of predicting positive is strictly less than predicting negative ($\ meast{Cost}(+) < \text{Cost}(-)$).

front: How do under-sampling and over-sampling techniques differ in handling class imbalance?
back: Under-sampling removes instances from the majority class, whereas over-sampling replicates or adds instances to the rare class.

front: Which confusion matrix outcomes bias the Precision metric?
back: Precision is biased towards True Positives ($C(\text{Yes}|\text{Yes})$) and False Positives ($C(\text{Yes}|\text{No})$).

front: Which confusion matrix outcomes bias the Recall metric?
back: Recall is biased towards True Positives ($C(\text{Yes}|\text{Yes})$) and False Negatives ($C(\text{No}|\text{Yes})$).

front: In hypothesis testing terms applied to confusion matrices, what corresponds to a Type I error ($\alpha$)?
back: A Type I error ($\alpha$) corresponds to a False Positive ($\text{FP}$), which is rejecting a true null hypothesis.

front: In hypothesis testing terms applied to confusion matrices, what corresponds to a Type II error ($\beta$)?
back: A Type II error ($\beta$) corresponds to a False Negative ($\text{FN}$), which is accepting a false null hypothesis.

front: What is the strategy of class-based ordering for handling imbalanced class rules?
back: It assigns higher priority to classification rules that predict the rare class.

front: What is another name for training errors?
back: Apparent errors: the errors committed on the training set.

front: Why can't training error be used to estimate generalization error?
back: It does not reflect how well the model performs on previously unseen records, especially when the model overfits.

front: What three approaches are listed for estimating generalization error during model selection?
back: Using a validation set, incorporating model complexity, and estimating statistical bounds.

front: What is the drawback of using a validation set for model selection?
back: Less data is available for training.

front: Besides the learning algorithm, what factors can a model's measured performance depend on?
back: The class distribution, the cost of misclassification, and the size of the training and test sets.

front: What extra information does repeated cross-validation provide?
back: An estimate of the variance of the generalization error.

front: When is stratified cross-validation especially important?
back: When classes are imbalanced and the sample is small.

front: What must a classifier produce in order to draw an ROC curve?
back: Continuous-valued outputs (scores) that can rank test records from most to least likely positive.

front: What trade-off does an ROC curve display?
back: Detection rate (TPR) against false alarm rate (FPR) as the classifier's threshold changes.

front: What is the formula for Precision?
back: $p = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$

front: Recall is the same quantity as which rate plotted on an ROC curve?
back: The True Positive Rate (TPR): $r = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$.

front: What is the formula for the F-measure?
back: $F = \frac{2rp}{r + p} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}$

front: Which confusion matrix cell is the F-measure NOT biased towards?
back: $C(\text{No}|\text{No})$, the true negatives; it depends on all other cells.

front: What implicit cost assumption does the standard Bayes rule (predict + if $p(+|x) > p(-|x)$) make?
back: That $C(+|+) = C(-|-) = 0$ and $C(+|-) = C(-|+)$: correct predictions are free and both errors cost the same.

front: With zero cost for correct predictions, what is the cost-sensitive threshold for predicting +?
back: Predict + if $p(+|x) > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}}$, where $C_{FP}$ and $C_{FN}$ are the costs of a false positive and a false negative.

front: What does it mean when two ROC curves cross?
back: Neither model consistently outperforms the other: one is better at small FPR, the other at large FPR.

front: What is the main distinction between agglomerative and divisive hierarchical clustering?
back: Agglomerative starts with individual points as clusters and merges them, while divisive starts with one all-inclusive cluster and splits it.

front: How is inter-cluster distance calculated in MIN (Single Link) hierarchical clustering?
back: It is defined as the distance between the two closest points belonging to different clusters.

front: Why can merge decisions made during hierarchical clustering be problematic in subsequent steps?
back: Once two clusters are merged (or split), the decision cannot be undone at later steps.

front: What is the relationship between Between-Cluster Sum of Squares (BSS) and Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WSS/SSE)?
back: For a fixed dataset, $\text{BSS} + \text{WSS} = \text{constant}$, meaning maximizing separation (BSS) minimizes cohesion error (WSS).

front: What is the standard time complexity for traditional hierarchical clustering algorithms, and to what can it be reduced?
back: Standard time complexity is $O(N^3)$, which can be reduced to $O(N^2 \log N)$ with optimized data structures.

front: How is inter-cluster proximity determined in the Distance Between Centroids approach?
back: It is measured as the distance between the centroid (mean) of the first cluster and the centroid of the second cluster.

front: How is inter-cluster distance defined in MAX (Complete Link) hierarchical clustering?
back: It is defined as the distance between the two most distant points belonging to different clusters.

front: How is a noise point defined in the DBSCAN algorithm?
back: Any point that is neither a core point nor a border point.

front: Why is Group Average considered a compromise between MIN and MAX linkage methods?
back: It averages all pairwise distances, so no single closest pair (MIN) or farthest pair (MAX) decides a merge. Like MAX it is less susceptible to noise and outliers than MIN, but it is still biased towards globular clusters.

front: How does K-means define each cluster center?
back: Each cluster is associated with a centroid, which is typically the mean of all points assigned to that cluster.

front: What structural limitations does basic K-means face regarding data distributions?
back: It struggles when clusters have differing sizes, differing densities, non-globular shapes, or when outliers are present.

front: How does increasing the number of clusters $K$ affect the Sum of Squared Error (SSE)?
back: The best achievable SSE never increases as $K$ grows, reaching zero when $K$ equals the number of points. So increasing $K$ is an easy way to cut SSE, but a good clustering with smaller $K$ can still have lower SSE than a poor clustering with larger $K$.

front: How does hierarchical clustering differ from partitional clustering?
back: Hierarchical clustering produces a set of nested clusters organized as a hierarchical tree, whereas partitional clustering produces a single flat division of non-overlapping subsets.

front: What is a partitional clustering?
back: A division of data objects into non-overlapping subsets such that each data object is in exactly one subset.

front: In cluster analysis, how are intra-cluster and inter-cluster distances optimized?
back: Intra-cluster distances are minimized, while inter-cluster distances are maximized.

front: What graphical technique is used to determine the parameters $\text{Eps}$ and $\text{MinPts}$ in DBSCAN?
back: Plotting the sorted distance of every point to its $k$-th nearest neighbor and identifying the sharp bend (knee) in the curve.

front: What is the space complexity of traditional hierarchical clustering for $N$ data points?
back: $O(N^2)$, because it requires storing the $N \times N$ proximity matrix.

front: How is inter-cluster distance computed in the Group Average approach?
back: It is computed as the average of all pairwise distances between points in the two distinct clusters.

front: Term: Dendrogram
back: A tree-like diagram that records the sequence of merges or splits in a hierarchical clustering algorithm.

front: What is a primary strength of the MIN (Single Link) distance metric in hierarchical clustering?
back: It can handle non-elliptical or arbitrarily shaped clusters.

front: What is a key practical advantage of using a dendrogram for cluster selection?
back: Any desired number of clusters can be obtained by cutting the dendrogram at the appropriate height level without re-running the algorithm.

front: How can K-means be adapted to capture natural clusters with non-globular shapes or differing sizes?
back: By finding a larger number of small sub-clusters ($K$ higher than true clusters) and merging them in a post-processing step.

front: How is the Silhouette Coefficient $s$ for an individual point $i$ calculated?
back: $s = \frac{b - a}{\max(a, b)}$, where $a$ is the average intra-cluster distance and $b$ is the minimum average distance to another cluster.

front: What shape bias does MAX (Complete Link) hierarchical clustering exhibit?
back: It tends to break large clusters and is strongly biased toward finding globular clusters.

front: What is the algorithmic time complexity of basic K-means per iteration?
back: $O(n \cdot K \cdot d)$ per iteration (every point compared with every centroid over all attributes), so $O(n \cdot K \cdot I \cdot d)$ in total for $I$ iterations — linear in $n$.

front: In fuzzy clustering, what restriction is placed on the membership weights of a single point?
back: A point belongs to every cluster with a weight between 0 and 1, and the sum of these weights across all clusters must equal 1.

front: Under what primary conditions does DBSCAN struggle to identify true clusters?
back: When clusters have widely varying densities or when dealing with high-dimensional data.

front: What defines a center-based cluster?
back: A set of objects where every object is closer (or more similar) to the center of its cluster than to the center of any other cluster.

front: What is the main weakness of MIN (Single Link) hierarchical clustering?
back: It is highly sensitive to noise and outliers, which can cause undesirable chaining of clusters.

front: In cluster validation, what does an ideal similarity matrix contain for a dataset?
back: An entry of 1 if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 if they belong to different clusters.

front: What formula measures cluster cohesion in K-means using Sum of Squared Error (SSE)?
back: $\text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \sum_{x \in C_i} \|x - m_i\|^2$, where $m_i$ is the centroid of cluster $C_i$.

front: What is a border point in DBSCAN?
back: A point that is not a core point itself, but falls within the $\text{Eps}$-neighborhood of a core point.

front: What defines a density-based cluster?
back: A dense region of points separated from other dense regions by regions of low density.

front: How does K-means++ improve upon random centroid initialization?
back: After a random first centroid, each new centroid is sampled with probability proportional to a point's minimum squared distance to the centroids already chosen, which favours widely separated starting points.

front: How does DBSCAN classify a point as a core point?
back: If it has at least a specified number of points ($\text{MinPts}$) within a defined radius ($\text{Eps}$), including the point itself.

front: What are the two broad purposes of cluster analysis named in the lecture?
back: Understanding (e.g. grouping related documents, genes/proteins with similar function, or stocks with similar price fluctuations) and Summarization (reducing the size of large data sets).

front: Why is the notion of a cluster said to be ambiguous?
back: The same points can reasonably be grouped into two, four or six clusters depending on the level of detail — clusters are "in the eye of the beholder".

front: What is the difference between exclusive and non-exclusive clustering?
back: In exclusive clustering each point belongs to exactly one cluster; in non-exclusive clustering a point may belong to several clusters, e.g. to represent multiple classes or 'border' points.

front: What is the difference between partial and complete clustering?
back: Complete clustering assigns every object to a cluster; partial clustering clusters only some of the data (e.g. leaving noise unassigned).

front: What does a heterogeneous set of clusters mean?
back: The clusters have widely different sizes, shapes and densities.

front: Which kind of clustering shares fuzzy clustering's characteristics?
